objection: Could the Bible have been changed to make Jesus divine?
answer:
This is a fair objection, and I'll grant its core factual premise readily: the Comma Johaneum is indeed a later insertion, absent from every Greek manuscript before the 15th century, and no honest defense of Christ's deity should lean on it. But the objection's force depends on an analogy — "if scribes inserted that, why not earlier claims?" — and the actual manuscript evidence runs the opposite direction from what the analogy predicts. We are not blind between 70 and 200 CE. The Rylands fragment (P52) of John dates to about AD 125, within a generation of composition, and the papyri P66 and P75 (c. 200) already contain "the Word was God" (John 1:1), "only-begotten God" (John 1:18), and Thomas' confession "My Lord and my God" (John 20:28) — over a century before Nicaea. If a scribe had "improved" a hazier original into these high statements, we'd expect to find that hazier original in the earlier layer of witnesses; instead the earliest layer we possess already contains the highest Christology, unmarked by any variant tradition suppressing it.

The case gets stronger still when you leave textual criticism for the history of devotion. Larry Hurtado showed that worship of Jesus — prayer, hymns, invocation of his name, baptism into him — erupted among Jewish monotheists within the very first years, not after centuries of scribal drift; Richard Bauckham showed the New Testament writers include Jesus within the unique identity of Israel's God using precisely the traditional Jewish markers for that identity. That is not the kind of thing a copyist quietly slips into a text decades later — it required a community-wide, apostolic-era conviction, evidenced independently of any single disputed verse. And Nicaea itself confirms rather than undermines this: the council did not vote deity into existence, it defended what Ignatius, the Philippian hymn, and Tertullian's already-settled Trinitarian vocabulary (c. 200) presupposed as ancient. So the real pattern in the evidence is the reverse of the skeptic's suspicion: the Comma is a late, isolated, textually indefensible addition we can identify and reject precisely because we have such deep, early, multiple manuscript lines to compare it against — the very abundance of witnesses that lets us catch a fourth-century-plus interpolation is what also lets us see that John 1:1, John 1:18, and John 20:28 belong to the earliest recoverable text, not a later layer.

# The Textual Problem

Look, you're asking me to trust documents copied by hand for *centuries* before any of them survive intact — and the earliest fragments we have show *thousands* of variants, some touching exactly the verses Christians cite for Jesus' divinity. The Comma Johanneum (1 John 5:7–8) — "the Father, the Word, and the Holy Spirit" — doesn't appear in any Greek manuscript before the 15th century, yet it's been used to prove the Trinity for a thousand years. If scribes were willing to slip that into the text, why wouldn't they have "improved" the earlier, hazier Gospels to make Jesus *explicitly* claim deity? The textual instability is real, and it happened *before* we can check it against earlier copies. How do you know the divinity claims weren't quietly inserted by motivated copyists between, say, 70 and 200 CE — before we have any witnesses?
